title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service's meeting recording feature is alleged to have captured private work conversations without informing participants their data would be used to train AI systems. The lawsuit claims the system recorded by default through integrations with calendar and video conferencing platforms, relying on a checkbox in a privacy policy rather than explicit consent at the moment of recording. Whether the company's anonymization process actually protected confidential information is not established.

The failure here is deployment without clear signaling to all affected parties. Participants in meetings recorded through automatic calendar integrations would not have seen a notice that their conversation was being captured for training data, only the account holder would have encountered a checkbox in a policy document. It would have taken prominent notification to each meeting participant, or a requirement for affirmative consent before recording began, to prevent the allegation that users were deceived.

Whether the company's practices actually violated privacy and wiretap laws is not established; that is the subject of the ongoing lawsuit.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission and using them to train its systems. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer, claims the company's Otter Notebook tool, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, records conversations by default without alerting participants that their data will be shared with Otter for artificial intelligence improvement. The lawsuit alleges this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and seeks to represent other California users whose conversations were unknowingly shared.

The company serves approximately 25 million users and has recorded over 1 billion meetings since its founding in 2016. While Otter's privacy policy mentions that users can grant permission through a checkbox to share transcripts for training purposes, the lawsuit maintains many users are still being deceived. Recent complaints on social media have highlighted instances where Otter's software joined meetings automatically through integrated workplace calendars and recorded discussions without participant consent. The suit questions whether Otter's method of anonymizing data before using it for machine learning effectively removes confidential information.
